q.q: Which of these is data rather than information?
o: 312 swimmers used the 25 m pool from 18:00 on Monday
Pupil 2087 scored 72% in the mock exam
The 07:42 bus from Enniskillen was 14 minutes late
q.why: Raw values with no context have no meaning on their own; the others give the values context.

q.q: Which shorthand best describes information?
o: Data + context + meaning
Data + rules + decision
Knowledge + validation
Data + storage + backup
q.why: Information is data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning. Applying rules to reach a decision describes knowledge.

q.q: How is knowledge produced?
o: By applying a rule to information so an informed decision can be made
By labelling raw data so that it has a meaning for the user
By storing information in a database where it can be searched
By checking that information is accurate and up to date
q.why: Knowledge comes from applying a rule, policy or experience to information to reach a decision or conclusion.

q.q: A shop's rule is to reorder milk when stock falls below 20 cartons. The system reports '2 L milk: 14 cartons in stock'. What is the knowledge here?
o: 2 L milk: 14 cartons in stock
Milk must be reordered now
The stock level was updated at 09:00
q.why: Applying the rule (below 20) to the information (14 in stock) gives the decision to reorder.

q.q: The value 25 could be a pool length in metres, a temperature in °C, a price in pounds or a mark. What does this show?
o: Data always has exactly one correct meaning
Information can exist without any data
Data has no meaning until context is added
Knowledge is the same as information
q.why: The same data can become quite different information depending on its context.

q.q: Why is 'Mark (%)' on its own NOT a good example of information?
o: It is a percentage, and percentages are always knowledge
It is a label with no value, so nothing has been given meaning
It has not yet been checked by a validation rule
It contains a symbol, so it can only be data
q.why: Information needs a value and its context, such as 'Pupil 2087 scored 72% in the mock exam'.

q.q: Which change turns the value 72 into information?
o: Storing 72 in an integer field in the database
Stating that pupil 2087 scored 72% in the mock exam
Converting 72 to the binary pattern 01001000
Checking that 72 lies between 0 and 100
q.why: Adding context (whose mark, which exam, what units) gives the value meaning.

q.q: Asked for an example of knowledge, a pupil writes: 'The second pool must open on Mondays.' Why might this lose the mark?
o: It is an example of data, because it has no units
It is information, because it mentions a day of the week
Knowledge can only be given as a number, not a sentence
It does not state the rule that was applied to the information
q.why: Mark schemes expect the rule being applied, e.g. 'open the second pool if more than 250 people use the main pool in an hour'.

q.q: Which statement about data is correct?
o: Data must be numeric before a computer can process it
Data has meaning on its own as soon as it is stored
Data becomes information once it has been validated
Data can be text, codes, dates, images or sound
q.why: Data is any raw values, not only numbers; it gains meaning when processed and given context.

q.q: In the leisure centre example, which is information?
o: Open the second pool from 18:00 on Mondays because usage exceeds 250
312 swimmers used the main pool between 18:00 and 19:00 on Monday
q.why: It is data given context, so it has meaning. The decision to open the pool is knowledge, and the bare value is data.

q.q: A vet doses a dog using a weight that was typed as 4 kg instead of 40 kg. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Relevance
Completeness
Accuracy
Reliability
q.why: The value was not recorded exactly as it is, so the information is inaccurate.

q.q: A head of department is sent every pupil's raw marks when she only needs the class averages. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Accuracy
Relevance
Completeness
Currency
q.why: Relevant information contains only what this user needs, at the right level of detail.

q.q: A bus app still shows last year's timetable, so passengers miss a new earlier service. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Being accurate
Being relevant
Being well presented
Being up to date
q.why: The information reflects an old situation rather than the current one (its currency).

q.q: A delivery note gives the street but not the house number. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Accuracy
Reliability
Completeness
Relevance
q.why: Something needed for the decision is missing, so the information is incomplete.

q.q: A council shows flood-risk data as 2 000 rows of grid references instead of a colour-coded map. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Accuracy
Presentation
Completeness
Currency
q.why: The data may be correct and complete, but the format makes it hard for users to understand quickly.

q.q: A shop orders extra stock because of a weather rumour on social media instead of the Met Office forecast. Which quality factor is lacking?
o: Relevance
Accuracy
Reliability
Completeness
q.why: Reliable information comes from a trustworthy, authoritative source.

q.q: What does the principle GIGO mean for an information system?
o: Good software can turn poor data into good output
Data is processed in the order in which it arrives
Graphical input always produces graphical output
Poor-quality input data will produce poor-quality output
q.why: Garbage in, garbage out: however good the software, bad data gives bad information.

q.q: A stock clerk types a quantity of 250 as 2500. What type of error is this?
o: Transposition error
Formula error
Transcription error
Bias in collection
q.why: A value mistyped or misread when copied is a transcription error; a transposition is two characters swapping places.

q.q: Why can adding more detail to make information complete sometimes reduce its quality?
o: Too much detail can bury the facts the user needs
More detail always makes information out of date
Complete information cannot be presented as a chart
Extra detail makes the source less reliable
q.why: There is a tension between relevant and complete: good information gives exactly the detail the decision needs.

q.q: A spreadsheet total accidentally leaves out one row. Which practice would best catch this?
o: Calculating the important total two ways and comparing
Applying a presence check to every cell in the column
Proofreading the column heading against the source
Rounding every value in the column to whole numbers
q.why: Cross-checking important totals by calculating them in two different ways reveals formula errors.

q.q: A shoe size field rejects 22 but accepts 9. Which validation check is this?
o: Range check
Type check
Length check
Lookup check
q.why: A range check tests that the value lies between a lower and an upper limit, here 1 and 15.

q.q: In C#, the code if (!int.TryParse(input, out int tickets)) reports a failure when 'three' is entered. Which check is this?
o: Type check
Range check
Format check
Presence check
q.why: TryParse fails if the input is not an integer, so it tests the data type.

q.q: A mobile number field rejects 0770090012 but accepts 07700900123. Which check is this?
o: Range check
Format check
Length check
Lookup check
q.why: The rejected entry has 10 characters instead of exactly 11, so a length check fails it.

q.q: An exam number must have the format LL9999 (two letters then four digits). Which entry passes the format check?
o: BT452Z
q.why: BT4521 has two letters followed by four digits; the others break the pattern.

q.q: A county field accepts only the six Northern Ireland counties and rejects 'Kildare'. Which check is this?
o: Range check
Format check
Lookup check
Type check
q.why: A lookup check compares the entry with a list of valid values.

q.q: An email field has a presence check only, and the entry 'x' is accepted. What should be added?
o: A second presence check on the same field
A format check on the email address
A range check on the email address
A type check that the email is text
q.why: A presence check only tests that something was entered; a format check tests the pattern of an email address.

q.q: A date field uses a format check for DD/MM/YY and accepts 47/19/26. What should be added?
o: A length check of exactly 8 characters
A presence check on the date field
Range checks on the day and the month
A type check that the date is text
q.why: 47/19/26 fits the pattern of digits and slashes; the day needs 1–31 and the month 1–12, or a routine that checks the date exists.

q.q: Which validation would correctly reject a time entered as 26:63?
o: Range checks: hours 0–23 and minutes 0–59
A length check of exactly five characters
A format check for the pattern 99:99
A presence check on the time field
q.why: 26:63 has five characters and fits the 99:99 pattern, so only range checks on each part will reject it.

q.q: What is the difference between a type check and a format check?
o: Type tests the pattern of characters; format tests the kind of data
Type tests the number of characters; format tests a list of values
Type tests that data is present; format tests it lies within limits
Type tests the kind of data; format tests its pattern of characters
q.why: Type is integer, text or date; format is a pattern such as LL9999.

q.q: What is validation?
o: An automatic check that input is sensible and obeys set rules
An automatic check that input is correct and accurate
A check that the input exactly matches the source document
A manual check of the entered data against the original form
q.why: Validation checks data is sensible or reasonable, not that it is true; matching the source is verification.

q.q: Using Modulus 11 with weights 5, 4, 3, 2, what is the checksum of the base number 5280?
q.why: 5×5 + 2×4 + 8×3 + 0×2 = 25 + 8 + 24 + 0 = 57. 48 uses the weights in reverse; 15 is just the sum of the digits.

q.q: Using Modulus 11, what is the check digit for the base number 5280?
o: X
q.why: The checksum is 57; 57 MOD 11 = 2; 11 − 2 = 9. 2 is the remainder, not the check digit.

q.q: The valid code 52809 is mistyped as 25809. Using weights 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, what does the check find?
o: Total 66, remainder 0, so the code is accepted
Total 63, remainder 8, so the code is accepted
Total 63, remainder 8, so the code is rejected
Total 57, remainder 2, so the code is rejected
q.why: 2×5 + 5×4 + 8×3 + 0×2 + 9×1 = 63; 63 MOD 11 = 8, not 0, so the transposition is caught.

q.q: Using Modulus 11 with weights 5, 4, 3, 2, what is the check digit for the base number 2001?
o: X
q.why: 2×5 + 0 + 0 + 1×2 = 12; 12 MOD 11 = 1; a remainder of 1 gives check digit X (standing for 10).

q.q: Using Modulus 11, what check digit does a checksum of 77 give?
o: X
q.why: 77 MOD 11 = 0, and a remainder of 0 gives check digit 0.

q.q: What weightings are used for the Modulus 11 base number 482913?
q.why: The rightmost digit has weight 2, rising by 1 to the left; six digits start at 7.

q.q: Why should a field holding a code with a Modulus 11 check digit be a string rather than an integer?
o: Integers cannot be multiplied by weightings
String fields are validated automatically
Integer fields are limited to four digits
The check digit may be the letter X
q.why: A remainder of 1 produces X, which an integer field cannot store.

q.q: Which errors is the Modulus 11 method designed to detect?
o: All errors in the source document the code was copied from
Any code that belongs to a different, valid customer
All single-digit errors and all transpositions of two digits
Bits flipped by interference during transmission
q.why: It catches mistyped and swapped digits; it cannot show the code belongs to the right person.

q.q: How do you show that a code with a Modulus 11 check digit is invalid?
o: Recalculate without the check digit; the remainder is 0
Add all the digits; the total is not a multiple of 10
Recalculate with the check digit at weight 1; the remainder is not 0
Count the 1s in its binary form; the count is odd
q.why: For a valid code the weighted total including the check digit is exactly divisible by 11.

q.q: What does a valid Modulus 11 check digit confirm about a code?
o: Its digits are consistent with each other
It belongs to the correct customer
It was entered twice and matched
The source document was correct
q.why: It only shows the number is internally consistent; a valid code may still be the wrong one.

q.q: A clerk counts the fee forms in a batch before they are keyed in. What is this count called?
o: Batch total
Control total
Hash total
Check digit
q.why: A batch total is a count of the documents in the batch.

q.q: The total of the fees paid on a batch of membership forms is calculated before entry. What is this called?
o: Hash total
Batch total
Control total
Check digit
q.why: A control total is the sum of a field whose total has a meaning, such as money paid.

q.q: The sum of all the member ID numbers on a batch of forms is calculated before entry. What is this called?
o: Control total
Batch total
Check digit
Hash total
q.why: A hash total is the sum of a field whose total has no meaning.

q.q: Which mistake would a hash total of member IDs detect but a batch total would miss?
o: Two forms both missed out of the batch
One form missed out of the batch
One form missed and a different form entered twice
One extra form added to the batch
q.why: The count of forms is unchanged, but the sum of IDs changes because the two IDs differ.

q.q: The manual hash total of member IDs is 11 556 but the computer's total is 9 239. What does this most likely show?
o: 2317 forms have been missed from the batch
The form for member 2317 has been missed
The form for member 2317 was entered twice
The control total of fees is £2317 too low
q.why: 11 556 − 9 239 = 2317; when exactly one document is missing the difference is its ID. A duplicate would raise the computer's total.

q.q: Every form in a batch shows the same fee of £30. Why would a control total of fees add little?
o: Control totals can only be used with whole numbers
The total would have no meaning, so it is a hash total
It tells you no more than the batch total does
A control total cannot be calculated by hand
q.why: If the field never varies, its total is just £30 × the number of forms.

q.q: One £30 form is missed and a different £30 form is entered twice. Which total would still detect this?
o: A hash total of member IDs
A control total of fees
A batch total of forms
None of the batch totals
q.why: The count and fees total are unchanged, but the IDs differ so their sum changes.

q.q: What is the main purpose of batch, control and hash totals?
o: To check that each field on a form is sensible
To check that a code number belongs to the right person
To detect bits flipped during data transmission
To check that every document in a batch is entered exactly once
q.why: They compare a manual total with the computer's total to find missed, duplicated or mistyped documents.

q.q: When are batch totals usually checked in a batch-processing system?
o: After the run, so errors can be corrected in the new master file
Before the run, so a bad batch is rejected before it updates the master file
During each real-time transaction while the user waits
Only when the master file is restored from a backup
q.why: Checking first stops a faulty batch corrupting the master file.

q.q: How are batch totals used to find an error?
o: A total worked out by hand is compared with the computer's total
The data is keyed in twice and the two copies are compared
Each field is compared with a file of valid values
A weighted sum of the digits is divided by 11
q.why: Before entry a clerk calculates the total; after entry the computer calculates it; a difference means an error.

q.q: What is the purpose of verification?
o: To check data has been entered accurately so it matches the source
To check data is sensible and within acceptable limits
To check the source document itself is correct
To check every document in a batch is entered once
q.why: Verification checks the copy matches the original; checking data is sensible is validation.

q.q: A website asks you to type your new password twice before saving it. What is this?
o: Validation by a presence check
Validation by a length check
Verification by proofreading
Verification by double entry
q.why: The two entries are compared automatically to catch keying mistakes.

q.q: When does double entry fail to catch an error?
o: When the user makes a different slip in each of the two entries
When the value entered is outside the allowed range
When the field is left blank on both occasions
When the user misreads the source and types the same wrong value twice
q.why: If both entries are identical, the computer sees no difference, even though both are wrong.

q.q: Why should proofreading ideally be done by someone other than the person who keyed the data?
o: People tend to see what they meant to type
Only a second person is allowed to edit the data
A second person can apply the validation rules
It halves the time needed to enter the data
q.why: A fresh pair of eyes is more likely to spot the actual mistakes.

q.q: After a school office enters GCSE entries for 180 pupils, a second member of staff checks the printed list against the subject choice forms. What is this?
o: Double entry
Proofreading
A lookup check
A batch total
q.why: Comparing the entry with the source by eye is proofreading, a verification method.

q.q: Which data is double entry best suited to?
o: Short critical fields such as account numbers
Long documents such as letters and reports
Every field on a large batch of forms
Values read automatically by sensors
q.why: Double entry doubles the keying workload, so it is kept for short, critical fields.

q.q: An online form shows 'Are these details correct?' with the data you typed before you submit. What is this?
o: On-screen confirmation, a verification method
A presence check, a validation method
A lookup check, a validation method
A hash total, a batch control method
q.why: Asking the user to confirm the entry matches what they intended is a form of verification.

q.q: After a file is copied to a backup drive, software compares the copy with the original. What is this an example of?
o: Validation
Verification
A range check
A check digit
q.why: Comparing a copy with its source checks it was copied accurately.

q.q: Why is double entry quick and consistent compared with proofreading?
o: Each value only needs to be typed in once
It also checks that the source document is correct
It applies the validation rules at the same time
The comparison is carried out automatically by the computer
q.why: The computer flags differences; proofreading depends on a person's judgement.

q.q: What is the main weakness of proofreading for large volumes of data?
o: It cannot be used on text or documents
It is slow and tired checkers miss errors
It needs the data to be keyed in twice
It is performed automatically by software
q.why: Proofreading depends on concentration, so long, repetitive lists cause errors to be missed.

q.q: A pupil's age is typed as 14 instead of 15. Why does validation not detect this?
o: Validation only runs on text fields, not numbers
Validation only runs after the data is stored
14 is still a sensible age, so it obeys the rules
Ages cannot be given a range check
q.why: Validation checks that data is reasonable, not that it is true.

q.q: A date field uses a day range check of 1–31 and accepts 29/02/2027. What limitation does this show?
o: Verification cannot detect errors in the source
The validation rules may be too simple
Presence checks accept any character at all
Check digits do not work on dates
q.why: 2027 is not a leap year, but the simple range rule does not know that.

q.q: A surname field with only a presence check accepts a single space. What does this show?
o: A presence check also tests the type of the data
Verification has failed to compare the source
The field needs a check digit to be added
A presence check only tests that something has been entered
q.why: Anything, even a space or 'x', passes a presence check.

q.q: A booking form was filled in on paper with the wrong date, and the clerk keys it in exactly as written. What will verification do?
o: Reject it, because the date is not sensible
Correct it, because the computer knows the date
Accept it, because the copy matches the source
Flag it, because double entry finds the error
q.why: Verification only checks the copy matches the source; an error in the source is copied faithfully.

q.q: Which error could pass both a range check and double entry?
o: An age of 470 typed the same way twice
A blank surname on both entries
The same wrong but sensible value typed twice
A password typed differently each time
q.why: It is sensible, so it passes validation, and identical both times, so it passes double entry.

q.q: Which statement about validation and verification is correct?
o: Validation guarantees that stored data is correct
Both reduce errors but neither can guarantee data is correct
Verification can find errors in the source document
Using both methods together removes every error
q.why: Validation misses valid-but-wrong values and verification misses errors in the source.

q.q: Which is the best way to complete the sentence 'Validation checks that data is…'?
o: correct and accurate
identical to the source document
true for the person it describes
sensible and within acceptable limits
q.why: Validation cannot check correctness; matching the source is verification.

q.q: Which method in the validation and verification process is carried out by people rather than software?
o: Double entry
Range checking
Lookup checking
Proofreading
q.why: Validation is automatic and double entry is compared by software; proofreading is a visual check by a person.

q.q: An organisation layers validation, verification and batch totals but still lets people view and correct their own records. Why?
o: Validation is not allowed for personal data
Verification only works when people check their own data
Batch totals cannot be used for personal records
Errors still get through, and correction is also a data protection right
q.why: No method eliminates errors, and UK data protection law gives people the right to correct their records.

q.q: A clerk misreads a 7 as a 1 on a form and types the same wrong value at both prompts of double entry. Which statement explains why it is accepted?
o: Verification only compares the two entries, which match
Validation always accepts numbers between 0 and 9
Double entry ignores single-digit differences
The value fails validation but passes verification
q.why: Both entries contain the same wrong value, so the comparison finds no difference.

q.q: What is data capture?
o: The process of checking data obeys set rules
The process of sorting a transaction file
The process of turning data into knowledge
The process of getting data into a computer system
q.why: Data capture is how data is input, whether keyed manually or read automatically.

q.q: A school needs to mark 2 000 multiple-choice answer sheets quickly. Which capture method is most suitable?
o: OMR
OCR
Manual keying
RFID
q.why: OMR reads marks in fixed positions quickly and accurately.

q.q: Which capture method turns the printed text on a scanned passport into editable text?
o: OMR
OCR
RFID
A data logger
q.why: Optical character recognition converts printed characters into text.

q.q: How does a barcode scanner help ensure each scan is read correctly?
o: The scanner reads each code twice and compares
The scanner looks the code up by line of sight
The barcode's check digit validates each scan
A hash total is printed on every barcode
q.why: The check digit is recalculated on each scan; a mismatch means a misread.

q.q: An environmental agency wants to record water levels on the Erne every 15 minutes, day and night. Which method is most suitable?
o: An OMR reader
Online forms
Sensors with a data logger
A barcode scanner
q.why: Sensors and data loggers capture data continuously and unattended in remote places.

q.q: Why are RFID tags suitable for ski passes?
o: They can be read by OCR from a printed photograph
They are free to produce and raise no privacy concerns
They are validated by a presence check on each reading
They can be read without line of sight, many at once
q.why: RFID needs no line of sight, so a pass in a pocket can be read; tags do cost money and raise privacy concerns.

q.q: What is the main advantage of online forms over keying data from paper forms?
o: No device or internet connection is required
Handwriting on the form can be read automatically
Data is captured at source and validated as it is entered
No validation is needed because the owner enters it
q.why: The person who owns the data enters it, so there is no re-keying, and each field is validated on entry.

q.q: Why does keying data from paper forms need validation, verification and batch totals?
o: It can only capture numbers, not text or dates
It needs specialist scanners that often misread
It captures data at source with no human input
It is slow and prone to transcription and transposition errors
q.why: Manual keying is cheap and flexible but people make keying mistakes.

q.q: In what way is manual data capture better than automated capture?
o: It is faster for very high volumes
It produces fewer keying errors
It needs specialist equipment
It can handle any data a person can read
q.why: Automated devices only capture the data they are designed for; manual capture is more flexible but slower.

q.q: What is a weakness of OMR?
o: It needs line of sight to RFID tags
It cannot read free text
It cannot read marks in fixed positions
It requires a check digit on every sheet
q.why: OMR only detects marks in set positions; forms must also be completed carefully.

q.q: Which application is best suited to batch processing?
o: Booking a concert seat
Controlling anti-lock brakes
Producing monthly payslips
Withdrawing cash from an ATM
q.why: Payroll is a large, regular job with no need for instant results.

q.q: In batch processing, why is the transaction file sorted before the run?
o: So the newest transactions are processed first
So it is in the same key order as the master file
So record locking can be applied to each record
So the master file is always kept up to date
q.why: The program reads both files in sequence, so they must be in the same key order.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of batch processing?
o: It needs a user present to process each transaction
The master file is only up to date straight after a run
It cannot be used for large volumes of data
It needs record locking to prevent double-booking
q.why: Between runs, new transactions wait in the transaction file, and errors are only found after the run.

q.q: An online concert booking system updates the seating plan as each seat is sold. What type of processing is this?
o: Real-time transaction (online) processing
Real-time control
Batch processing
Multithreading only
q.why: Each transaction updates the master file while the user waits; there are no sensors.

q.q: A car's anti-lock braking system reads wheel sensors and adjusts the brakes within milliseconds. What type of processing is this?
o: Real-time control
Real-time transaction processing
Batch processing
Multi-user processing
q.why: Sensor input is processed within a guaranteed time so the output affects the next input.

q.q: How does the response time of real-time control usually compare with real-time transaction processing?
o: Seconds, rather than milliseconds and guaranteed
Milliseconds and guaranteed, rather than seconds
Overnight, rather than within a few seconds
The same, as both are real-time processing
q.why: Control systems must respond within a guaranteed very short time; transaction users wait a few seconds.

q.q: Two agents try to sell the same flight seat at the same moment. What prevents double-booking?
o: Batch totals
A feedback loop
A hash total
Record locking
q.why: Record locking stops two users updating the same record at once.

q.q: Which feature is typical of real-time control rather than real-time transaction processing?
o: Users at terminals waiting a few seconds for a response
A feedback loop where the output affects the next input
Record locking to stop two users updating a record
A transaction file sorted into key order
q.why: Real-time control uses sensors in a feedback loop; the others belong to transaction or batch processing.

q.q: Which is an advantage of batch processing?
o: The master file is always up to date
Errors are found while the user is still present
It can run when the system is quiet and is easy to schedule
Each transaction is processed as it happens
q.why: Batch jobs run unattended, often overnight, and are easy to schedule, back up and audit.

q.q: A Northern Ireland hospital trust needs a system to sound an alarm the moment a patient's heart rate becomes dangerous. Which processing method is needed?
o: Real-time control
Batch processing
Real-time transaction processing
Overnight processing
q.why: Sensor input must be processed within a guaranteed time because a late response is dangerous.

q.q: How does multitasking work on a single-core processor?
o: The processor switches rapidly between programs using time slices
Several programs genuinely run at the same instant
Each program is given its own separate core
Many users share the processor at once
q.why: Each process gets a short time slice of a few milliseconds, so the programs appear to run simultaneously.

q.q: Thirty pupils are logged into the school file server at the same time. What does this describe?
o: Multithreading
Multitasking
A multi-user system
Batch processing
q.why: Many users share one system's resources, each with their own session and permissions.

q.q: A web browser downloads images while also responding to the user's scrolling. What does this describe?
o: Multi-user
Multitasking
Batch processing
Multithreading
q.why: One program is split into threads that run concurrently.

q.q: What is a thread?
o: A separate path of execution within one program, sharing its memory
A separate program with its own memory and its own user
A short time slice given to a process by the scheduler
A user session on a shared multi-user server
q.why: Threads are parts of one program that run concurrently and share that program's memory.

q.q: Why can multithreading improve performance on a multi-core processor?
o: Threads do not need any memory to run
Threads can genuinely run in parallel on different cores
Each thread gets a faster clock speed
Threads stop the need for time slices
q.why: On several cores, threads of one program can run at the same time rather than taking turns.

q.q: A game calculates physics in one thread and draws the screen in another. What is this an example of?
o: Multitasking
Multithreading
Multi-user
Real-time transaction processing
q.why: One program has several threads running concurrently.

q.q: Which task must a multi-user operating system carry out that a single-user one need not?
o: Keep each user's data and session separate and secure
Switch between programs using time slices
Display a graphical user interface
Load device drivers for peripherals
q.why: With many users sharing resources, separation, security and fair sharing are essential.

q.q: A pupil streams music while writing an essay and downloading a file on the same laptop. What does this describe?
o: Multitasking
Multi-user
Multithreading
Real-time control
q.why: One user runs several programs that share the processor.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three terms?
o: Multitasking: many users; multi-user: many programs
Multithreading: many programs; multitasking: many threads
Multi-user: one program; multithreading: many users
Multitasking: many programs; multithreading: one program, many threads
q.why: Multitasking is several programs, multithreading is several threads in one program, multi-user is several people.

q.q: Why does a multi-user booking server use record locking?
o: To give each user a fair time slice
To stop two users corrupting the same shared record
To split each booking into threads
To keep users' passwords encrypted
q.why: Two users must not update the same record at once, or one update could be lost.
